title: Marble Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Marble wells have a 100-foot median depth, 12 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $12,500-$22,000.
h1: Marble, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land around Marble means dealing with mountain bedrock, limited well records, and real variation from one lot to the next. Within five miles of Marble, Colorado, DWR records include 498 permitted wells. Of those, 264 are recorded as constructed, 272 report a total depth, and only 90 report a pump yield.

The records are useful for setting expectations, but they do not guarantee what a new well will produce. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, so nearby results matter more than a broad county average. Check the actual neighboring wells before buying or pricing a build.

sections.heading: Marble well depths reflect fractured mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Marble is 100 feet. The middle half runs from 55 to 200 feet, while the deepest recorded well reaches 500 feet. About 46% of wells are under 100 feet, and another 43% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The remaining 11% are in the 300-to-600-foot range.

That spread is important when reviewing a drilling bid. A nearby shallow well may not predict your result if the fracture network changes across the property. Permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 482 wells, with only 2 tied to alluvial aquifers and 10 to Mancos. Granite and gneiss can produce water through fractures rather than a uniform layer.

sections.heading: Most Marble wells make useful household flow
sections.html:
Among the 90 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 5.2 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 44% report between 5 and 15 gpm, and 38% report more than 15 gpm.

Only 1% of reported wells are under 1 gpm, while 17% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. That is a favorable record for ordinary household use, but the sample is much smaller than the permit count and reported yields are not a promise for an unbuilt well. Ask for the neighboring well construction reports, pump test information, and intended use before relying on a yield assumption.

sections.heading: Water levels are commonly within the upper part of the well
sections.html:
The 32 wells reporting static water levels show a median depth to water of 41 feet. The middle half runs from 18 to 50 feet. Static water level is not the same as well depth or pumping yield: it describes where water stood when measured, while pumping can lower the level temporarily.

There are not enough reported water-level records here to establish a reliable decade-by-decade decline or rise. Do not treat the median as a site-specific guarantee, especially on fractured bedrock. A driller can evaluate the local geology, and a buyer can compare nearby permits and request current information where available.

sections.heading: Marble permit history shows long-term drilling activity
sections.html:
Permit activity is established around Marble, with records beginning in the 1960s and the newest permit issued in 2024. The records list 7 permits in the 1960s, 47 in the 1970s, 71 in the 1980s, 168 in the 1990s, 78 in the 2000s, 49 in the 2010s, and 35 in the 2020s.

The most active names in these records are Shelton Drilling Corporation with 183 wells, Collins Drilling Co with 107, and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc. with 41. Those records can help identify local experience around Redstone, Snowmass Village, and the upper Crystal River area, but an old permit still needs to be checked for construction details and current condition.

sections.heading: What a new Marble well may cost
sections.html:
Marble drilling means working in fractured mountain bedrock, commonly granite or gneiss. The cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 100 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $6,500 to $10,000.

A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at $12,500 to $22,000. That is a planning range, not a fixed bid. Depth, access, casing and grout requirements, difficult rock, water testing, and site layout can change the total. Ask for separate line items so you can see what is included and what happens if the hole must go deeper.

sections.heading: Check mines, septic layout, and low-yield risk before closing
sections.html:
The mapped area has 192 historic mine features within about 10 miles of Marble. It has 0 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the same mapped search. Those findings do not replace a water test. Historic mining, local geology, and old site activities still deserve review, particularly if a property is near a mine feature.

Most permits are for domestic or household use at 87%, but a well permit does not solve every building issue. Confirm the permitted use, septic reserve area, driveway access, and space for the well and septic system before designing a home. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed. A Colorado exempt household-use well also has a 35 gpm pumping limit.

sections.heading: Use nearby permits to plan a Marble purchase or build
sections.html:
Before making an offer, pull the closest DWR well permits and compare depths, reported yields, static levels, construction, and dates. The local record is strongest for basic household wells, not necessarily for irrigation or larger demands. If the lot is near Redstone, Snowmass Village, or another mountain community, use the closest comparable wells rather than assuming results from farther away in the valley.

For a new build, have a driller review access, pad location, casing and grout, power routing, storage, and the septic layout together. Budget using the finished-system range, then confirm the contractor's exclusions. If an existing well is present, test the water, verify the permit and use, inspect the equipment, and ask for a current production evaluation before treating it as a dependable supply.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Marble, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Marble is 100 feet. The middle half ranges from 55 to 200 feet, 46% are under 100 feet, and the deepest record is 500 feet. Because most permits identify fractured-bedrock aquifers, a neighboring well is useful evidence but cannot guarantee the depth on your lot.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Marble?
faq.a: Among the 90 Marble-area wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 5.2 to 15.0 gpm. About 1% report under 1 gpm, while 38% report more than 15 gpm. These figures describe reported wells, not a guaranteed result for a new hole.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Marble?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 100-foot median depth, drilling alone is estimated at $6,500 to $10,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $12,500 to $22,000. Site access and difficult rock can change the bid.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Marble, Colorado?
faq.a: The mapped search found 0 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. It also found 192 historic mine features. Those records are not a water-quality guarantee. Test an existing or new well for the conditions relevant to the property, especially near historic mining activity.

faq.q: Are Marble wells affected by a dropping water table?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a reliable water-level trend. Only 32 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 41 feet and a middle half from 18 to 50 feet. That is a snapshot of reported measurements, not evidence of a rising or declining table. Ask for current local measurements when evaluating a property.
